title: Narada and the good company
hookLine: Narada's start as a servant boy, and the company of the true
carry: the company of the true changes you

lines: HOLY MEN, STAYING FOR THE RAINS.
cards: This week you went to the temple, walked around the shrine, met the priest, sang, and watched two people take seven steps. Under all of it: other people.
Narada, the wandering sage who sings his way through every world, once told how he began. In a past life, he said, he was the small son of a maidservant.
One year, as the rains came, a group of holy men arrived to stay where his mother worked, and the boy was sent to look after them. Today: satsang.

teach.b: Every day of the rainy season, he brought the holy men water, swept up, and listened while they sang and talked about God. That's all. No vow, no books.
He just stayed near people who loved God, and, the Bhagavata Purana says, the love rubbed off. Before they left, they taught him.

That boy became Narada, who carries his veena through the worlds singing Vishnu's names, and who in the old stories turns up exactly when someone needs good company: he sheltered Prahlada's mother, and he set the boy Dhruva on his path.
That's satsang, the word you met on day twenty. Sat means true, real, what actually is.

teach.h: SAT + SANG: THE COMPANY OF THE TRUE.
teach.b: Sang means company. Satsang is the company of the true, and in Hinduism it isn't just pleasant, it's a practice.
Remember Shankara's chain from that day: good company leads to letting go, letting go to clarity, clarity to a steady mind, and a steady mind to freedom.
Many follow a shape: singing, a reading or a short talk, silence, prasad, and tea afterward, which is where people become friends.
Start with what's established and public: a temple, a long-running group, a friend's family.
And good company welcomes you and lets you leave; a group that pressures you, asks for big money, or cuts you off from family isn't satsang. Sit in the back, sing what you can, stay for the tea.

how: Many Hindus attend satsangs, regular gatherings at temples, homes or community halls that usually include devotional singing, a reading or talk, silence and prasad, followed by tea and conversation; serving at them is part of the practice.

o: gathering in the company of the true and good
a group trip to a well-known pilgrimage site
a silent retreat, spent alone with a guru

games.q: the company of the true — tap the pairs.
p: a servant boy who served holy men and listened
the first link to freedom, in Shankara's song

s: Narada became a sage by studying alone for years
in his telling, it began with one rainy season of serving holy men and listening.
and sang means company: satsang is the company of the true.
a good group pressures you to keep coming back
good company doesn't grab. it welcomes, and lets you leave.

games.q: you're a small boy whose mother works in a house. holy men arrive to stay for the rainy season, and you're told to look after them. what do you do?
o: bring them water, and listen to every song.
ask for a blessing, then go play.
games.why: the boy served and listened for the whole season, and the love rubbed off. he became Narada. that's satsang: the company of the true changes you.

practice: Think of one place near you where people gather like this: a temple, a community hall, a campus group, a relative's living room. If you don't know any, think of one person you could ask.

Choose one to try in the next month, and picture the evening: shoes off, a spot at the back, someone passing you a lyric sheet. Then, like the boy who carried water, picture one small way to help: stacking chairs, pouring the tea.

wordCard.voice: Satsang. The company of the true: people gathering to sing, read, sit in silence and share tea, and the good company that changes you. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit satsaṅga: company with the true or the good. Often written सत्संग.

carryVoice: Your line: the company of the true changes you. Narada started by carrying water. Tomorrow, Diwali begins.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 1.5–6 (Narada's past life serving sages during the rains); 7.7 (Narada shelters Prahlada's mother); 4.8 (Narada guides Dhruva)
Bhaja Govindam (attributed to Shankara), verse 9: good company leads to non-attachment, clarity and liberation
